The tool uses try cast, which turns forty point zero zero into the decimal forty, minus five into minus five, and n slash a into NULL, rather than failing. A plain cast, with Spark four's ANSI mode on, would fail the whole job on that one bad value. Try cast is right, but it creates NULLs, so the next habit is to count them. Second, NULL itself. The tool counts rows where the amount equals NULL, and gets zero. It counts rows where the amount is NULL, and gets one. A comparison with NULL is never true, not even NULL equals NULL, so a filter written with equals silently finds nothing. Third, time. The tool reads the same text, the first of October at nine fourteen, as a timestamp under two session time zones, UTC and New York, and prints each as seconds since the epoch. The two numbers differ by fourteen thousand four hundred seconds, which is four hours. The same text meant two different instants, depending only on a setting. Fourth, nested data. Two orders worth sixty-five in total each carry an array of items. Exploding the arrays, one row per item, and then summing the amount gives one hundred and five, because order one's amount was repeated for each of its two items. The table on the right lists the traps, and the list gives the habit that prevents each. Use try cast, and count the NULLs it makes. Write IS NULL, never equals NULL. Store times in UTC, and convert only to display them. And aggregate before you explode, or deduplicate after. Next, the join mistake that inflates a total.

Silver will enrich each order with its store's city, by joining to the stores reference, which has now arrived in the project as a small CSV: seven is Leeds, nine York, twelve Hull. A join looks harmless, and this lesson shows the one way it goes wrong silently. The tool starts from the five completed orders that silver will finally hold, worth one hundred and seventy in total. It joins them to the stores reference. Then it makes a second copy of the reference in which York appears twice, the way it would if a reference file were resent, and joins to that. The terminal shows a real run. Joined to the clean stores: five rows, one hundred and seventy. Joined to the copy with York twice: six rows, one hundred and eighty-five. Nothing failed. Order four, the one York order, matched two store rows, so it became two rows, and its fifteen was counted twice. The table on the right is the arithmetic: one duplicate key in the reference, one extra row, fifteen too many. The rule is in the list. A join multiplies: a row that matches n rows on the other side becomes n rows. There is no error, just a bigger total, and a total that is too big usually looks perfectly plausible. So check the key before you join. The last lines of the tool are that guard: group the reference by store ID, and keep any key that appears more than once. It finds store nine, twice. A pipeline should run that check, and stop or quarantine, before it trusts a reference table. And the final habit is to state the grain of every table: one row per what? The stores reference is one row per store. Once that is written down, a second York is a broken contract rather than a surprise. Next, how to keep one row per order when bronze has several.

Bronze can hold several rows for one order: order four sent twice, and order six first as pending, then later as completed. Silver keeps one row per order, the latest, and the tool for that is a window function. The highlighted window partitions the rows by order ID, and orders each partition by source file, newest first. Our files arrive in name order, a, b, c, d, so the latest file is the latest information. Row number then numbers the rows in each partition, one, two and so on, and keeping row number one keeps the latest row for every order. The terminal shows a real run for the two orders that matter. Order four: number one comes from file c, number two from file b. They are identical, so keeping either is correct, but keeping c is the rule. Order six: number one is the completed row from file d, and number two the pending row from file b. The later status wins. The second half of the tool shows the failure this rule prevents. It orders order four's rows by amount alone. Both rows have the same amount, fifteen, so the ordering has a tie, and row number has to break it somehow. The tool shuffles the same two rows twelve different ways and records which file was kept each time. The last line shows both files were kept, on different runs. With a tie, the survivor depends on the order the rows happened to arrive in, which changes between runs. Because this is chance, this step's exact output can differ, but more than one survivor is the point. The table on the right sums it up, and the list gives the rule. Partition by the key. Order by what latest actually means. Make that order total, with no ties, by adding a tie-breaker that is unique for every row, like the source file here. Then the same input always keeps the same row. Next, the quality rules that decide which rows reach silver at all.

Now silver gets its rules, and they live in the new quality module in the editor. The rules are data: a list of pairs, a reason and the SQL condition that fails a row. Amount unreadable, when try cast left the amount NULL. Amount not positive, when it is zero or less. Unknown store, when the join to the stores reference found no city. And bad status, when the status is not one of the three we know. The reason function at the bottom turns that list into a single column: for each row, the first rule it fails, in order, or NULL if it passes them all. The new silver module uses it. Its checked function types every bronze row, joins it to its store, and adds the reason. The terminal runs a tool that shows the rows that failed, from a real run. Order seven: amount unreadable. Order eight: amount not positive, minus five. Order nine: unknown store, fifteen. Eight rows passed, and three were quarantined. Silver's build function, which the last lesson of this course runs, writes those three to a quarantine table, and keeps the latest passing row per order in silver orders. The table on the right is the reconciliation that this makes possible. Eleven events. Six reach silver. One is order four's identical resend. One is order six's superseded pending row. And three are in quarantine, each with its reason. Eleven equals six plus one plus one plus three, and every event is accounted for. The list says why the design looks like this. One list of rules, read in order, means the first failure wins and every bad row gets exactly one reason. A failing row keeps that reason, so the owner of the source can fix it. Quarantine is a table you can query and count, not a line in a log that scrolls away. And the reconciliation is checked on every run. Next, the gold table, and the promises it makes.

Gold is what other people read, so it is built as a contract with them rather than as the output of a query. The new gold module in the editor starts with the table's definition. Gold sales has one row per city. City may not be null. Orders counts completed orders, and sales sums their amounts, as a decimal. Every column carries a comment that says exactly what it means, and the table itself has a comment stating its grain and that it is rebuilt every run. The build function creates the table if it does not exist, adds a check constraint that sales may never be negative, and then fills it with insert overwrite: completed orders from silver, grouped by city. Insert overwrite replaces the rows but keeps the table, so the comments and the constraint survive every rebuild, where dropping and recreating the table would lose them. The terminal runs a tool that builds silver and gold and reads the contract back, from a real run. Describe table shows the three columns, their types, and their comments, which is what someone exploring the catalog would see. Then the tool tries to break the contract, inserting a row for Leeds with sales of minus five. The write is refused, and the error names the constraint and the value. Spark's logs about the failed task are folded above it. The table on the right lists each promise and what enforces it: one row per city, by the grouping; only completed orders, by the filter; never negative, by the check constraint; and the meaning of every column, by its comment. The list says why this matters. Readers depend on gold's shape, so changing it is a decision, not a side effect of editing a query. The grain is written down, not implied. And a broken promise fails the write, before a wrong number ever reaches a report. On Databricks, the same comments and constraints show up in Unity Catalog for every reader. Next, the whole flow, end to end.

The pieces are built, and the new run module joins them into one flow, which the terminal runs with python dash m retail dot run. Its main function does four things in order. It ingests whatever has landed into bronze. It builds silver and its quarantine. It builds gold. And then it checks itself, which is the part most pipelines leave out. The terminal shows a real run. First the reconciliation, computed rather than asserted. Eleven events equals six in silver, plus one resent, plus one superseded, plus three quarantined. The resent count comes from comparing all rows with distinct rows in bronze. If any of those numbers changed without a reason, this line would show it. Then gold itself, the first real version of the table the whole course has been building towards. Hull, one order, eighty. Leeds, three orders, seventy-five. York, one order, fifteen. And the last line is the second check: the completed amounts in silver add up to one hundred and seventy, and so do the sales in gold. Detail equals summary. If a join had inflated a total, or a filter had dropped a row, those two numbers would disagree. The table on the right is the flow at a glance: eleven rows in bronze, three in quarantine, six in silver, and three cities in gold, totalling one hundred and seventy. You may remember gold from the first course totalled one hundred and sixty. The difference is order six. In the first course's sample it was still pending. Here, file d brought the update that it completed, and silver kept the latest row, so its ten now counts. That is the system working as designed, not a discrepancy. The list ends with the question this raises. This flow rebuilds silver and gold from all of bronze every time. That is simple and correct, but what happens when rows keep changing, and arriving late, and the data is too large to rebuild? Next, handling change.

Until now, every run read every file. That is simple and always correct, but its cost grows with history, not with what is new. This course is about handling change, and it starts with the cheapest change: new rows arriving. The sample here is ten order events in four small JSON files, which land one at a time, the way a store would send them. The tool does two things after each file lands. The highlighted read is a recompute: it reads every file so far and counts the rows. The stream below it is incremental: the same files, read as a stream with a checkpoint, so each run reads only what arrived since the last one. The terminal shows the difference. After the first file both read three rows. After the second, the recompute reads six and the stream three. After all four, the recompute has read twenty-seven rows in total, and the stream ten, exactly the ten events. The list says what that saving rests on. The source must only append: a file, once landed, never changes. The checkpoint remembers what was already read, which is the stream's only memory. And recompute work grows with history, while incremental work grows with arrivals. A change to a row that was already read is not an arrival, so a plain incremental read never sees it. That is source CDC, later in this course. Next, what happens when events arrive late.

Ten events, but they do not arrive in the order they happened. Each carries its own time, the event time, and this frame sums sales into ten-minute windows by that time, not by when a file landed. The highlighted watermark is the stream's rule for late data: wait ten minutes behind the latest event time seen, and no longer. Each batch reads one file. The terminal shows each batch's watermark and what it wrote. The first batch has none yet. After it, the latest event was nine fourteen, so the watermark becomes nine oh four. As later events arrive, the watermark moves to nine thirteen, nine twenty-one and nine thirty-four. A window is written once the watermark passes its end, so in append mode each window appears exactly once, when it is final. The nine o'clock window is written in batch two as ninety-five. The ten past window in batch three, as one hundred and ten. And the twenty past window, ten, in the last batch. The table on the right follows the late events. Order ten happened at nine oh six but arrived in batch two, while its window was still open, so it is counted in the nine o'clock window. Order twelve happened at nine oh two but arrived in batch three, after its window had already been written and closed, so it is dropped, silently. And order four was sent twice, so the ten past window counts it twice: a watermark does not deduplicate. The list gives the trade. A longer wait catches more late events, and writes every window later. Next, removing that duplicate, and what it costs to remember.

To drop order four's resend, a stream has to remember every order it has already seen. That memory is called state, and this frame measures it. The tool deduplicates the same ten events twice, on the order ID and its event time. Once with no watermark, and once with the ten-minute watermark from the last section. The terminal prints, for each, how many events were kept and how many keys the state held after each batch. With no watermark, nine of ten are kept: the resend is dropped. But the state grows with every batch, three, five, seven, nine, and it never shrinks, because nothing ever says a key can be forgotten. On a real stream that runs for months, that is a stream that eventually runs out of memory. With the watermark, the state rises and falls, three, three, four, three, one. Once a key is older than the watermark, no duplicate of it can still be accepted, so it can go. Eight of ten are kept this time, because the watermark also drops late order twelve. The list says why the event time is part of the key. The watermark expires state by event time, so a deduplication key without the event time column can never expire. State is the price of asking, have I seen this before. The watermark is what keeps that price bounded. Next, the same idea with two streams: a join.

Orders are paid separately, and payments arrive on their own stream. This frame joins the two, an order to a payment made within fifteen minutes of it. Both streams carry a watermark, and the join condition carries a time bound, the highlighted between. Together they tell each side how long to keep its rows waiting for a match. The tool runs the join twice, as an inner join and as a left outer join, and prints each batch's output. Orders one and two match in the first batch, four and five in the second, with order four twice because it was sent twice, then eleven and thirteen. The two joins agree until the very last batch, where the outer join writes order ten as unpaid. Order ten was paid at nine thirty, twenty-four minutes after it was placed, so it can never match within fifteen. The outer join can only say so once the watermark has passed the end of its window, which is why that row comes last. The table on the right covers the others. Order six was never paid, but its fifteen minutes have not yet passed the watermark when the files run out, so it is still waiting in state. And order twelve was too late to enter the join at all. The list is the rule. Each side keeps its rows until no match can still come, and the time bound plus the watermarks decide when that is. Without a bound, both sides would be kept forever. Next, the folder that holds all of this state: the checkpoint.

A stream stops: a deploy, a crash, a cluster restarted overnight. What it does next depends entirely on its checkpoint. The tool runs a windowed sum over the first two files, stops, lands a third file while it is stopped, and starts the same query on the same checkpoint. The terminal shows it ran batches zero to two, and after the restart, batches three and four. It did not start again from zero, and it read the file that landed while it was down, once. The listing below shows what the checkpoint holds, and the table explains each folder. Offsets record what each batch was going to read, before it runs. Commits record which batches finished. Sources record which files were read. State holds the open windows, split by partition. And metadata holds the query's identity. The last part of the tool changes the query and keeps the checkpoint, adding the store as a second grouping key. The run is refused: the state store's key schema is not compatible with the one on disk. The state was built for windows alone, and cannot be reinterpreted as windows per store. The list sums up which changes a restart survives. Stopping and starting, yes. Files landed meanwhile, yes. Many changes to filters or new columns are fine. A change to what the state is keyed by is not. That needs a new checkpoint, and a backfill to rebuild the state from the source. Next, what happens when a crash lands between writing a batch and committing it.

The checkpoint commits a batch only after its write has returned. So if the stream crashes after writing but before committing, the restarted stream runs the same batch again. That is called at-least-once, and this frame shows what it does to two kinds of sink. Inside foreach batch, the tool writes every batch twice: appended to one table, and merged into another on the order ID and event time. After writing batch two, it crashes on purpose, once. The terminal shows the state after the crash: eight rows in the append sink, and seven in the merge sink, because the merge already dropped order four's resend. Then the stream restarts. Batch two runs again, then batch three. The append sink now holds twelve rows for ten events: batch two's rows are there twice. The merge sink holds nine, the nine unique events, exactly what it would hold if nothing had crashed. The table on the right is the comparison. The list says where the responsibility sits. The checkpoint guarantees that no batch is lost. It cannot guarantee that a batch is written only once, because the write and the commit are two different steps. Making a replayed batch harmless is the sink's job. A merge on the key does it. An append does not. Next, change records from a source, where the order of arrival cannot be trusted at all.

So far, every event was a new fact. A change feed from a source system is different: it describes changes to rows we already hold. The till system sends change records for orders one to three. Each record has an operation, insert, update or delete, and a sequence number that orders the changes for one order. The table on the right shows the eight records, in three batches, as they arrived. The third batch is the hard one. It holds an update for order one with sequence two, which arrived after sequence three, so it is late. And it repeats order three's insert, after order three was deleted. The first line of the terminal applies the records naively, in arrival order, with a plain merge and real deletes. The result is wrong twice. Order one shows pending, because the late update overwrote the newer one. And order three is back, resurrected by the repeated insert. The editor shows the project's answer, source retail cdc. The highlighted merge updates a row only when the record's sequence is newer than the one the row already holds. A delete only sets a flag, so the row and its sequence survive, and a late insert cannot undo it. Before merging, apply keeps the newest record per order within the batch. The last three lines apply the batches in order, reversed, and replayed twice. All three give the same table: order one completed, order two completed, order three deleted. Order of arrival no longer matters. Next, what to do with the history these changes describe.

The change records describe more than the current state. They describe a history, and a table can keep it or not. The two ways are called slowly changing dimensions, type one and type two. The tool reads the same records, drops the repeat, and leaves seven distinct changes. Type one, the first query, keeps only the current row per order: the newest record by sequence, with deleted orders removed. The terminal shows two rows, order one at forty-five, completed, and order two at twenty-five, completed. Order three is gone. Type two, the second query, keeps a row for every version, with the sequence it became valid from and the sequence it stopped being valid. Order one has three versions: pending at forty from one to two, pending at forty-five from two to three, and completed from three, still open. Order two has two. And order three has one version, valid from one to two, closed by its delete. The delete adds no row of its own. The table on the right gives the difference as two questions. Type one answers what is true now. Type two answers what was true at any time. The list adds the warning that matters most. The versions are ordered by sequence, not arrival, using the same guard as before. And type two must be chosen while the history still exists, because a type one table has already thrown it away. Next, a feed that sounds the same and answers a different question.

Course five turned on Delta's change data feed, and this course has used a source's change records. They sound alike, but they describe different things, and this frame puts them side by side. The tool creates the sequenced table with the change feed on, applies the source's three batches through the project's apply function, and then reads the table's feed back. The source sent eight records. The table's feed holds nine rows, grouped in the terminal by version and change type. Version one has three inserts. Version two has three pre-images and three post-images, one pair per changed row. Order three's delete is one of them, because in our table a delete is an update of its flag. And batch three, with the late update and the repeated insert, changed nothing in our table, so the feed has no rows for it. That is the point of the table on the right. Source CDC says what the source did, including the changes we chose to ignore. The table's feed says what our table did, only what the merge actually changed. The list says which to read. To build silver from a source, read the source's records. To build gold incrementally from silver, read silver's feed, because it already holds only real changes. Next, a worked recovery, where the history is gone.

The last section brings the course together on one bad day. The sequenced table from the last section has its change feed, but its files are vacuumed with zero hours of retention, the way a too-eager cleanup job might. The terminal shows vacuum deleting the old files. Then the change feed from version one is read again, and fails: the file does not exist. The history is gone. The table itself still reads, and the next line shows it intact: order one completed at sequence three, order two completed at sequence two, order three deleted. So the current state survived, but every question about the past now has no answer. The last part rebuilds the table from the source's raw change records, all eight at once, duplicates and late ones included, through the same apply function. The rebuilt table equals the original. That works for one reason only: the raw records were still there. The table on the right is what was left after the vacuum. The list collects the course's three defences. Duplicates need an idempotent sink. Out-of-order changes need a sequence guard. And lost history needs the raw records, kept in bronze, because a rebuild is only ever possible from what was kept. That is why retention is a recovery decision, not only a storage cost. Next course, the same pipeline declared instead of written: Lakeflow declarative pipelines.

Course seven built the flow as an application: the run module calls bronze, then silver, then gold, in that order, and each step writes its own table. That is imperative code. We decide the order, the writes, the checkpoints, and what to do when something fails. Databricks offers a second way to say the same thing, Lakeflow declarative pipelines, and the right-hand file shows our flow in it. This file is documented, not run, because pipelines need a workspace, and its names were checked against the documentation's summaries. Read it from the top. The pipelines module is imported as dp. Each function returns a DataFrame and is marked with a decorator. Bronze orders is a table, read as a stream from the landing volume with Auto Loader. Silver orders is a table too, with three expectations, the quality rules, written as decorators. And gold sales is a materialized view. Notice what is missing. No function writes anything, and no function is called. The table underneath says who decides what. With run dot py we call the steps in order. With a pipeline, the order comes from what each function reads: silver reads bronze by name, so bronze runs first. We keep our own checkpoints; the pipeline keeps its. We create and write our tables; the pipeline keeps declared datasets in step with their definitions. Bad rows go to our quarantine code, or to expectations. And a failed run is ours to rerun, or the pipeline retries the update. The list keeps it honest. The transformations inside are the same Spark as before. What changes is who runs them. Next, the three kinds of dataset a pipeline can declare.

A pipeline declares datasets, and there are three kinds, each with a different job. The code on the left is the same datasets in pipeline SQL, again documented and not run. A streaming table, like bronze orders here, reads a stream: on each update it processes only the rows that are new since the last one, the way our checkpointed streams did. A temporary view, typed orders, stores nothing; it is a named step that other datasets in the same pipeline can read. And a materialized view, gold sales, reads its inputs as a batch and holds a result that is kept correct as those inputs change. The table on the right lines them up. A streaming table reads a stream, adds only new rows, and suits bronze and silver. A materialized view reads a batch, holds a correct full result after every update, and suits gold, joins and sums. A temporary view stores nothing and is a step in between. The list is how to choose. If the source only appends and each row needs to be read once, a streaming table. If the result must stay right as its inputs change, including updates and deletes upstream, a materialized view. The platform may refresh a materialized view incrementally or recompute it, depending on what it can prove about the query. Either way the answer is the same; only the cost differs. Next, how these definitions become a graph.

Nothing in the pipeline file draws an arrow, yet the pipeline knows the order to run things in. This frame shows the graph our three definitions produce. Bronze orders reads the landing volume with cloud files. Silver orders reads bronze orders as a stream, by name. Gold sales reads silver orders, and joins the stores reference. Each of those reads is an edge. The stores table is read by its full three-part name from outside the pipeline, so it is a source, not a node the pipeline manages. Underneath on the left is the second project file this course adds: the bundle resource that deploys the pipeline, documented and not run. It names the pipeline, the catalog and schema its datasets are published to, serverless compute, and continuous false, which means a triggered pipeline: each update processes what is there and stops. Its library is the pipelines file. Course twelve deploys it with the rest of the bundle. The table on the right gives the four words the documentation uses. A dataset is a table or view the pipeline owns. A flow is what writes into a dataset; usually it is implied by the definition, but one streaming table can take several flows, such as two sources appended into one table. A sink is a flow whose target is outside the pipeline, such as a message bus. And an update is one run of the whole graph. The list adds the rule that makes this safe: a cycle is refused before anything runs. Next, the quality rules, declared as expectations.

In course seven, the quality rules lived in the quality module, and silver's build sent failing rows to a quarantine table. In a pipeline the same rules are expectations, and each expectation has a policy for what happens when a row fails it. There are three. Warn keeps the row and records the violation. Drop removes the row and records it. Fail stops the update. This frame cannot run a pipeline, so the tool in the editor is a model: plain Spark applying the project's own rules to the eleven bronze events, by the documented semantics of each policy. It proves nothing about the platform, and the frame says so. The terminal shows the rules one by one: the unreadable amount fails one row, order seven; the negative amount fails one, order eight; the unknown store fails one, order nine; and no status is invalid. Then the policies. Warn keeps all eleven and records three violations. Drop keeps eight and drops three. Fail stops at the first violation and writes nothing. The table on the right gives each policy's decorator, what it keeps, and whether the pipeline reports metrics for it. According to the documentation, warn and drop produce counts; fail produces the stop. The list says what the model shows that matters. Drop loses the row, and keeps no table like our silver quarantine. When a dropped row matters, keep a quarantine table as well, by declaring a second dataset with the opposite condition. And fail is for the rules that must never be broken. Next, what a streaming table assumes about its source.

A streaming table processes only new rows. That works because its source only appends. This frame runs, locally and for real, what happens when that assumption breaks. The tool creates a small Delta table with two pending orders and streams it into a copy. The first run copies two rows. Then the source table updates order one to completed, a row the stream has already passed on, and the stream runs again. It is refused, with Delta's error that the source table has changes it cannot ignore. Delta will not guess. An update rewrites a file the stream has already read, and the stream has no way to turn that into new rows without duplicating or losing something. The next line sets skip change commits. The stream continues, and the copy still holds two rows: the update never arrives, and order one stays pending in the copy. The last line inserts order three, and the stream reads it: three rows. Skipping skips only the commits that changed existing rows. The table on the right is the rule, and it is the same rule a streaming table in a pipeline follows: inserts are read, updates and deletes stop the stream, and skipping them goes on without them. So the list gives the choices. Skipping keeps a stream running and loses the change. When a source really changes rows, handle it as change data, in a CDC flow, which is the next section. Or read it into a materialized view, which recomputes and is right by construction. Next, AUTO CDC.

Course eight wrote change handling by hand, in the cdc module: a merge on the key, guarded by the sequence, with deletes as flags. A pipeline can declare the same thing with AUTO CDC, the current name for what used to be apply changes into. The code on the left is documented, not run. It declares a streaming table, orders history, and a flow into it from the stream of order changes. Keys says what identifies a row: the order ID. Apply as delete when says which records are deletes. Sequence by says which record is newer: the sequence number. Columns except leaves the operation and sequence out of the result. And stored as SCD type two keeps every version. The table underneath maps each clause to the code it replaces. Keys is the merge condition on the order ID. Sequence by is the guard that a record must be newer than the row. Apply as delete is the deleted flag. The newest record per key within a batch, which our apply did with a row number, is handled by the flow. And SCD type two is the valid from and valid to of course eight. The table on the right shows what the result would hold, and it is illustrative: course eight's real versions, written in the documented column names, start at and end at. The list is the important part. Declaring it does not make the decisions for you. The key and the sequence are still yours. A tie in the sequence still needs a tie-breaker. Type one or type two must still be chosen before history is lost. And the changes still have to arrive first. Next, refreshes, and what they replay.

A pipeline runs in updates, and there are three ways to start one, documented here. An ordinary update runs the whole graph: streaming tables take only their new rows, and materialized views are brought up to date. A refresh of selected datasets runs only the ones you name. And a full refresh clears streaming tables and reads their sources again from the very beginning. The first two are routine. The third is the dangerous one, and the table underneath shows why with this project's own source contract. A full refresh of bronze orders rebuilds it from whatever the landing volume still holds. If the volume holds every file ever sent, bronze comes back the same. But course six's contract says the stores' order files are kept for thirty days. Then a full refresh leaves only the last thirty days, and everything older is gone, from bronze and from everything built on it. And a file deleted since it was read is simply missing. The list is the rule that follows. A full refresh rebuilds from what the source still holds, and bronze may be the only copy of older data. So protect such tables from a reset. The documentation describes a table setting for that, and its name, pipelines dot reset dot allowed, is unverified here and must be checked before use. When a downstream result is wrong, refresh the views downstream, which are computed from bronze, rather than bronze itself. Next, how to read what an update did.

Every pipeline keeps an event log: one row for each thing that happened, every update, every flow, every expectation. It is a table, and the query on the left reads it through the event log function for one of the pipeline's tables. This query is documented, not run, and the log's exact schema is unverified, so it must be checked before it is relied on. The table beside it is illustrative. It is not output from a platform. It shows what an update would report if one rule, the positive amount, were a fail rule instead of a drop rule, built from this course's own numbers. The update starts. Bronze orders completes with eleven rows. Silver orders fails. And the update fails. The table underneath walks that back to a cause. Which update failed: the update progress events, in time order. Which dataset: the flow progress event that says failed. Which rule: the failure's details name it, amount positive. Which row: the rule's condition leads to bronze, and order eight, with an amount of minus five, from course seven. And what was written: nothing for silver, because a fail rule stops the update before it writes. The list says what the log is for. Every update, flow and expectation leaves an event. Warn and drop leave counts, which is how you would know that three rows were dropped on a quiet day. Fail leaves the stop. And because it is a table, you can query it, and alert on it. Next course, how the pipeline runs every day: jobs and schedules.

So far, we ran every step by hand. In production, something else has to run the project every day, in the right order, and say clearly what happened. On Databricks that is Lakeflow Jobs, and this frame shows the project's job, as a bundle resource in the resources folder. It is documented, not run: jobs need a workspace, and the field names were checked against the documentation's summaries and must be checked again before use. Read the file from the top. The job is called retail daily. It takes two parameters, the run date and the number of rows we expect. It is scheduled with a cron expression, half past six every morning, London time. It runs as retail job, the service principal from course four. And it has six tasks. Ingest, transform, validate and publish each run an entry point of the project's wheel, which course twelve builds. Rows ok is a condition task: it compares two values and runs nothing. Alert runs only if something upstream failed. The graph on the right is what the depends on lines declare. Ingest feeds transform and the row check. Transform feeds validate and the alert. Publish needs both validate and a true outcome from the row check. The table lists the kinds of task a job can run, according to the documentation: a notebook, a wheel's entry point, a pipeline update like course nine's, a SQL query on a warehouse, a condition, or one task for each item of a list. The next sections run the rules of this graph, as a model, with real tables. Next, the values that flow into and between tasks.

A job passes small values around, and this frame shows the two kinds. Parameters come in from the job: the run date, and the expected number of rows. Task values are set by one task and read by another. Since there is no workspace, the editor shows a model of the documented rules, with real Spark inside each task. Ingest reads the landed files, writes bronze, and sets a task value, rows read. The condition task, rows ok, compares that value with the expected rows parameter, and records its outcome. And publish depends on validate and on rows ok's outcome being true. The terminal runs the job twice. With all three files, ingest reads eight rows, eight is at least eight, the condition is true, and publish succeeds. With file c not yet landed, ingest reads six rows, the condition is false, and publish is excluded. Excluded is a different state from skipped: nothing failed, a condition simply said no, so the run itself is not a failure. Ingest and validate still succeeded. The table on the right summarises who sets each value and who reads it. The list shows how the documentation writes these references: double braces around job dot parameters dot run date, and around tasks dot ingest dot values dot rows read. The call that sets a task value from code is in the documentation as dbutils dot jobs dot task values, and its exact spelling must be checked before use. The rules here are a model; the eight and six are real counts. Next, what starts a run at all.

A job runs when something triggers it, and the documentation describes four kinds, across the top. Scheduled, by a cron expression, like ours at half past six. File arrival, when new files land in a watched location. Table update, when a source table changes. And continuous, where a new run starts as soon as the last one ends. The choice is a trade between freshness and compute, and the table underneath makes it concrete with one hypothetical assumption: each run takes ten minutes. That is not a measurement, and no prices are quoted. Run once a day, and gold can be up to a day and ten minutes old, for ten minutes of compute a day. Hourly, up to an hour and ten minutes old, for four hours a day. Every fifteen minutes, up to twenty-five minutes old, for sixteen hours. On file arrival, about ten minutes after each file lands, for one run per arrival. And continuously, ten to twenty minutes, all day. The list gives the way to choose. Ask the readers how fresh is fresh enough, because each step fresher costs more runs, and runs are compute. File arrival suits sources that land at irregular times. An incremental job, like ours, which reads only new files, makes frequent runs cheap, because a run with nothing new does almost nothing. For retail daily, the stores send their files overnight, so once a day at half past six is enough. Next, what happens when a task fails.

When one task fails, every task after it has to decide what to do, and that decision is part of the job's design. The editor shows the model's rule, written from the documentation. For each task, it collects the states of its upstream tasks. By default, a task runs only if all of them succeeded. A task with a run if of at least one failed runs only if one of them failed. If a task does not run, it is excluded when a condition said no, and skipped otherwise. The terminal runs the job with a fault injected into transform. Ingest succeeds. Transform fails. Validate is skipped, because its upstream failed, and so is publish. Rows ok succeeds, because it depends only on ingest. And the alert succeeds: its rule is at least one failed, and transform did. The last lines are the run's log, the fault and the alert it caused. The table on the right gives the reason for each state. The list draws the lesson. All succeeded is the default, so one failure stops everything after it, which is what you want for publish: nothing reaches the readers from a broken run. A failure path, like the alert, has to be designed in, with a run if. Skipped and excluded mean different things: upstream failed, against a condition said no. And the run as a whole fails, and says which task broke. This is a model of documented rules, with real Spark in each task, and it proves nothing about the platform. Next, how to recover from a failure without making things worse.

After a failure there are three ways back, and each has a different effect on the data. This frame runs all three on the model, with real Delta tables. First, a repair. The documentation says a repair run re-runs only the tasks that failed or were skipped, and keeps the ones that succeeded. The terminal shows it: bronze has eight rows, published has one row of one hundred and sixty, and ingest ran once. Second, a full rerun, which starts every task again, ingest too. With an append ingest, bronze now holds sixteen rows: every file was loaded twice. Silver still holds six, but only because transform happens to use distinct. That is luck, not design. With a merge ingest, keyed on the file and the order, bronze stays at eight. Third, a retry after a write that committed. Publish writes its row and then fails, as a timeout after the write would. The task is retried once. With an append, the day now has two rows in the published table. With a merge on the run date, it has one. The table on the right puts the three side by side. The list states the rule the documentation is clear about: the platform does not make tasks idempotent. A repair helps only when the failed task's own write is safe to run again. Every write that a retry or rerun can reach should be a merge or an overwrite on a key, so that running it twice gives the same table as running it once. Next, whose permissions a run uses.

Every run is somebody. Whatever a task reads or writes, it does with the privileges of the job's run as identity, and our job runs as retail job, the service principal from course four. This frame checks that before the first scheduled run, using course four's grant model, which reads the project's grants file. The model prints its matrix first: finance reads gold only, engineers read and write bronze and silver, and retail job reads bronze and silver and writes silver. Then the tool asks what this job actually needs. Ingest writes bronze: refused, because retail job lacks modify on the bronze schema. Transform writes silver: allowed. Publish writes gold: refused, lacking use schema and modify on gold. Course four's grants were written for a job that only refined bronze into silver. This job also ingests and publishes, and the model found both gaps before the first run at half past six, rather than at it. The table on the right names the three identities. Ana is a person, who writes and deploys the project. Retail job is a service principal, used by every scheduled run. And finance is a group, reading gold. The list says what follows. Run as decides whose privileges every task uses, so it should be a service principal, not the person who happened to deploy the job, whose access may change. The fix is a decision: grant modify on bronze and gold to retail job, or split the job so each part runs with only what it needs. Either way, each grant should name the task that needs it. Next, the whole flow, orchestrated.

The last frame puts the course together. The model runs a job whose tasks are the project's own modules: ingest calls bronze ingest, transform builds silver, validate checks that every event is accounted for, and publish builds gold. Validate is new. It reads the counts, and fails the run if silver and quarantine hold more rows than bronze has events, so that a broken run can never reach gold. The tool runs the job on two days. On the first day, all four tasks succeed, validate counts eleven events, six in silver and three bad, and gold totals one hundred and seventy, the number from course seven. On the second day, no new files have landed. All four tasks run and succeed again, and nothing changes: still eleven events, still one hundred and seventy. The table on the right explains why a second run is harmless. Ingest is repeat-safe because of the checkpoint from course six: it reads only files it has not seen. Transform rebuilds silver whole. Validate only reads. And publish replaces gold with insert overwrite. Compare that with the last section, where an append ingest doubled bronze on a rerun. The list draws the line between the two halves of the work. The job decides when tasks run and in what order. Each task decides what it writes, and how safely. Validate stands between the data and its readers. The real job is the YAML file from the first section, and course twelve deploys it with the bundle. Next course, making it fast and cheap.

Making a pipeline fast starts with something that has nothing to do with speed: a baseline that proves the answer is right. This course uses one million generated orders. The tool on the left makes them, from the helpers in the fast lab module, and the data is generated by hashing each order's number, never at random, so every run produces exactly the same million rows. It spreads them over forty writers with no particular order, which is how a table looks before anyone has thought about its layout, and saves it as fast orders. The terminal shows the baseline. One million rows, and the sum of the amounts, fifty million, four hundred and ninety-seven thousand, four hundred and thirty-six. That sum is the checksum: every layout and every trick in this course must keep exactly this answer, because a faster query with a different answer is simply wrong. The table holds twenty-four files, and a query for store seven opens all twenty-four of them. Nothing tells Spark which files could be skipped. The list is about what a local measurement can honestly say. Counts are exact and repeatable: files opened, rows per partition, tasks per stage. Timings are not. This is one laptop, with other work on it, so this course quotes no seconds and claims no speed-up. Every number in it is a count of work, which is what a faster configuration actually reduces. Next, how to read the evidence of where the work goes.

Before changing anything, look at what the engine actually did. Spark records it in the Spark UI, and the same numbers are available from the UI's REST API, which is what the tool reads. The first half moves eighty percent of the orders onto one store, store seven, and shuffles them into four partitions by store. Then it asks the API for that stage's task summary: the rows each task read, at the minimum, the quartiles and the maximum. The terminal shows it. The smallest task read thirty-six thousand rows, the median sixty-four thousand, and the largest eight hundred and fifty-five thousand, thirteen times the median. That shape is skew: one task does almost all the work while the others wait. The second half aggregates just one thousand rows three ways and reads how many tasks the aggregation used. With the default two hundred shuffle partitions, two hundred tasks, for a thousand rows, which is overhead, not work. With four partitions, four tasks. And with two hundred partitions but adaptive query execution on, one task: adaptive execution looked at the real sizes after the shuffle and merged the tiny partitions. The table on the right keeps the skewed quantiles. The list says how to use evidence like this. A maximum far above the median is skew. Hundreds of tasks for a few rows is too many partitions. On Databricks the same evidence appears in its Spark UI and in query profiles, which are documented here, not run. Next, compute: what to buy, and when not to.

The most obvious way to make something faster is a bigger machine, and the most expensive. This frame is documented, not run, and it is about eligibility, not recipes. The three cards are the levers the documentation describes. Classic compute: you choose the node type, the number of workers or autoscaling, and you pay while it sits idle until it times out. Serverless: the platform chooses and starts the compute, you pay for what runs, and some settings are fixed for you, with availability varying by region and feature. And Photon: a native engine underneath Spark that runs the same SQL and DataFrame code, speeds up the operators it supports, and falls back to Spark for the rest. Whether a particular workload benefits was not confirmed here, so check the query plan rather than assume. The table is the reason to measure first. Each row is a symptom from the last section. One task thirteen times the median is skew, and a bigger machine does not help, because that one task still does the work. Two hundred tasks for a thousand rows is too many partitions, and more machines only add overhead. Every file opened is a missing layout, and more machines help only a little, at a price. A sort spilling to disk, from too little memory, is the case where bigger machines really do help. The list sums it up. Serverless removes the sizing decision, not a bad data layout. Photon changes the engine, not the shape of the plan. Next, joins, shuffles and skew.

Most of the work in a slow query is data moving between machines, the shuffle. The tool joins the million orders to a fifty-row stores table and sums sales per store, and it reports two things from the physical plan: which join Spark chose, and how many shuffles it needs. The first line is the default: a broadcast hash join, with one shuffle. The stores table is small, so Spark copies it to every task, and the million orders never move for the join; the only shuffle is the group by. The next line turns broadcasting off. Spark falls back to a sort-merge join, and now there are three shuffles: both sides of the join, then the group by. The answer is the same, as the line says, but a million rows crossed the network twice more to get it. The second half is skew. With stores spread evenly, the largest of four partitions holds about three hundred and twenty thousand rows. Move eighty percent of the orders onto store seven, and the largest partition holds eight hundred and fifty-five thousand, because every row of one key must land in the same partition. Salting adds a random-looking number, from zero to sixty-three, to the key, so store seven is split sixty-four ways, and the largest partition falls back to three hundred thousand. The parts are summed afterwards. The list collects the rules. Broadcast small sides. Know that a hot key concentrates work in one task. Salt it, or let adaptive execution split a skewed join, which was turned off here so the plans stay fixed. Next, small files.

A table's files are a cost of their own. Each one has to be listed, opened and read separately, so a table of many small files is slow even when it holds little data. The tool writes the same million orders with two hundred writers. To make a million rows behave like a much larger table, the fast lab module lowers optimize's target file size to four hundred kilobytes; that is the only setting changed. The terminal shows the result: one hundred and twenty-eight files, and a query for store seven opens every one of them. Then optimize, Delta's compaction command, rewrites them into fewer, larger files. Afterwards there are twenty-five files, the query opens twenty-five, and the table still holds exactly one million rows. The table on the right puts the two side by side. The list explains where small files come from and what compaction does not do. Many small writes, like a stream committing every few seconds, or many writers, like our two hundred, make many files. Optimize rewrites them into fewer. The old files stay in the table's storage for time travel until vacuum removes them, as course five showed. And notice that the store seven query still opens all twenty-five. Compaction makes fewer files, but every file still holds rows of every store, so none can be skipped. Skipping needs the data arranged by the column you filter on, which is the next section.

Delta keeps the minimum and maximum of each column for every file. If a query asks for store seven and a file's stores run from twenty to thirty, that file is skipped without being opened. That only works if the data is arranged so files hold narrow ranges, and this frame compares five ways of arranging the same million orders. The terminal's table shows files, and files opened for two filters. With no layout, twenty-four files, all opened for either filter. Compaction alone, two files, both opened. Z-order by store, nineteen files, and the store filter opens just one. Liquid clustering by store, also nineteen files and one opened. But a filter on the customer opens all nineteen on both, because a layout helps the columns it was built for. Partitioned by order date, a folder per day: seven hundred and twenty files, because each of twenty-four writers wrote into each of thirty days, and the store filter opens all of them. A filter on one date opens twenty-four, the files of that day. Partitioning by customer, a column with a thousand values, makes two thousand files. The last line checks the baseline: every layout still holds one million rows and the same sum. The table on the right is the store seven column. The list draws the lessons. Partitions help only filters on the partition column, and a column with many values makes far too many files. Liquid clustering, according to the documentation, replaces both partitioning and Z-order for new tables, and its columns can be changed later. Next, letting the platform do this maintenance.

The last two sections ran optimize by hand. On Databricks, the documentation describes predictive optimization, which decides when maintenance is worth running and runs it for you. This frame is documented, not run. Across the top is what it runs: optimize, for compaction and clustering; vacuum, to remove old files past retention; and analyze, to keep the statistics the query planner uses. The table underneath says where it applies, as the documentation's summaries describe it, to be checked again before relying on it. It works on Unity Catalog managed tables. It does not run Z-order. It is not available in every region. It is on by default for accounts created from the eleventh of November twenty twenty-four. And cluster by auto, where the platform chooses the clustering columns itself, needs it enabled. The list says what stays yours even when it is on. Choosing what to cluster by, unless you hand that choice to auto. Setting retention long enough for time travel and for recovery, which course eight showed is a recovery decision, not only a storage one. Maintaining external tables, which it does not manage. And checking that it actually ran: its operations are recorded in a system table, so you can query what it did rather than assume. Next, putting the measurements together into a comparison you can defend.

The last section puts this course's measurements into the form a decision usually needs: cost. The tool is plain arithmetic, and its first lines say exactly what is assumed. Every input is an assumption except one. It assumes three seconds to open and read a file, two machines, one cost unit per machine-hour, and an hourly job, twenty-four runs a day. None of these are prices, and none were measured. The one measured input is the number of files each layout opened for the store seven query, from section six: twenty-four with no layout, two with compaction only, one with liquid clustering, and seven hundred and twenty when partitioned by date. The terminal multiplies them out. No layout costs nought point nine six units a day. Compaction alone, nought point nought eight. Liquid clustering, nought point nought four. And partitioned by date, twenty-eight point eight, seven hundred and twenty times the work for this query. The table on the right labels every input, measured or assumed. The list is how to make such a comparison defensible. Check the same checksum first: one million rows and the same sum, or the faster layout is simply wrong. Then compare the measured work, files opened per query. Cost is that work multiplied by assumptions, so state every one. And re-measure on the platform before deciding, because a laptop's file count is evidence, and its prices are not. Next course, shipping the project and operating it.

The last part of the course is about shipping the project and running it for real. It starts with where code lives. Everything the pipeline does is in the package, source retail, and this section adds one more module to it: jobs, the editor's file. It holds the job's entry points, one per task of the job from course ten. Each is a few lines. Ingest builds a session and calls bronze ingest. Transform calls silver build. Validate reads three counts and stops the run if silver and quarantine hold more rows than bronze received. Publish calls gold build. They contain no logic of their own; the logic is in the modules every lesson has used. The terminal shows the boundary between local and remote. Listing the package shows its modules. Then a search for the three things that make a session local: the local master, the Hive metastore, and Delta's pip helper. All four matches are in one file, session dot py. On Databricks, the runtime provides the session, so that one file is the only thing that differs. The table on the right says where each kind of code lives. The logic in the package, which runs everywhere. The job's steps in jobs, which run as wheel tasks. Exploration in notebooks, and lessons and checks in tools, which are run by hand. One more change, highlighted in the explorer: silver's choice of the latest row is now its own function, latest, so the tests in section three can test it alone. Next, packaging the code as a wheel.

A job on Databricks runs code from a wheel, a Python package built as one file. The editor shows what describes it, the project file. Its dependencies are empty, on purpose: Spark and Delta come from the runtime, and locally from the requirements file. Pytest is an optional extra, for testing only. And the scripts section names the five entry points from the last section, ingest, transform, validate, publish and alert, which the job's wheel tasks call by name. The terminal builds the wheel for real, with pip, and then the tool reads what is inside it. The wheel is retail lakehouse, version nought point one. Its code is the package's modules. It requires nothing, except pytest with the test extra. It does not require PySpark or Delta. And it declares the five entry points. The table on the right splits what comes from the wheel from what comes from the runtime. The modules and entry points come from the wheel. Pytest only with the extra. PySpark, Delta, Python and Java from the runtime. The list explains why that split matters. A wheel that declared PySpark could install a second copy, which would fight the one the runtime already provides. So the wheel carries only our code, and the versions we test against locally should match the runtime's, which course two showed how to read. Next, the tests that run before any of this is deployed.

The project now has tests, and the terminal runs them with pytest: seven passed. They are three kinds, and the table on the right counts them. Four unit tests, in the quality test file, each check one rule or one function on rows written in the test itself: an unreadable amount, a negative amount, an unknown store, and that latest keeps the row from the newest file. One integration test, in the editor's file, runs the whole flow on files a to d and checks that gold totals one hundred and seventy. And two data-quality tests check the tables it built: that every one of the eleven events is accounted for, six in silver, one resend, one superseded, three quarantined, and that completed sales in silver equal the total in gold. A session fixture runs all of them in a scratch copy of the project, so the tests never touch the project's own tables. The second command shows why tests like these matter. The tool contains a bug that raises no error: it keeps the oldest file's row instead of the newest. Run, it would quietly publish wrong data. Next, the bundle that does the deploying.

Everything that makes up the project in a workspace, its job, its pipeline, its wheel, and who may run and read them, can be declared in one file in the repository, and deployed from it. Databricks calls this a bundle; the product is Declarative Automation Bundles, once called Databricks Asset Bundles. The file on the left is the project's bundle. It is documented and not validated, because validating a bundle needs a workspace, so every field must be checked before use. Read it from the top. The bundle is named retail lakehouse. It includes the resources folder, which holds the job from course ten and the pipeline from course nine. It builds one artifact, the wheel, the same way section two did. It declares a variable, the catalog. And it has three targets. Dev is in development mode, which the documentation says prefixes names per user and pauses schedules, and uses a dev catalog. Staging has its own catalog. Prod is in production mode, runs as the retail job service principal, and lets finance view. The table on the right lists each part and what it says. The list draws the point. The project's code, its jobs and its pipelines live in one folder and change in one commit. Validate checks the bundle, and deploy puts it into a workspace. And the same files deploy to every target; only the target's settings differ. Next, moving a change from dev to production.

A change should reach production by one path, and the same path every time. The chain across the top is that path, as documented. An engineer works in dev, with per-user names. A push starts CI. CI deploys to staging, a copy of production with its own catalog. And after an approval, the same commit is deployed to prod, where it runs as retail job. The file underneath is a sketch of the CI step, a GitHub workflow, and it is not run here, so every step is unverified. It checks out the code, sets up Python and Java, installs the requirements and the test extra, and runs the seven tests locally first. Only then does it install the Databricks command-line tool, validate the bundle against staging, and deploy it there. The credentials are a service principal's OAuth secret, stored as repository secrets, never in the file. The list on the right is about rolling back, which is where code and data differ. Rolling back code is easy: deploy the previous commit again. But that does not undo what the bad version wrote. A bad table can be restored with Delta's restore, from course five. Silver and gold can be rebuilt from bronze. And the rule that prevents most of this: promote nothing that skipped staging. Next, how to see what production is doing.

Once the job runs every morning without anyone watching, the evidence of what it did has to be somewhere you can query. The query on the left reads the documented job run timeline system table for the retail daily job, with the table's name to be re-checked before use. The result beside it is illustrative, built from course ten's failure path: two good days around a day when transform failed. The table underneath lists four kinds of evidence, as documented. Logs say what one run printed. Metrics say how much and how fast, in the Spark UI and query profiles from course eleven. Lineage says what fed what, from Unity Catalog in course four. And system tables keep every run and every cost, in schemas called system. The list makes the point that matters most for a data pipeline. A green run can still publish wrong numbers: a job that succeeds while the data is wrong is the failure that monitoring of the job alone never sees. So log the reconciliation on every run, eleven equals six plus one plus one plus three, so a change in it is visible. Keep the pipeline's expectation counts from course nine. And alert on a breach of what the readers were promised, not only on a failed task, which is the next section. Next, objectives, measured.

An incident should start with a number, not with a feeling that something is off. This section measures two objectives on the sample day, and both objectives are illustrative: they are the kind of promise a team would agree with its readers, not targets from any real company. The first is quality: at least ninety-five percent of events pass the rules. The second is freshness: silver is no more than fifteen minutes behind the newest file that landed. The tool measures both from the data itself. Quality: eight of eleven events pass, seventy-two point seven percent, against ninety-five. Breached. Freshness: the newest file landed at nine fifty, and the clock reads ten twenty, so thirty minutes, against fifteen. Breached. Two details keep this honest. The clock is fixed at ten twenty, so the result repeats on every run. And the landing times of the files were set by this step's setup for the example; on the platform they would be the files' real arrival times. The table on the right holds the two measurements. The list says how objectives turn into incidents. Agree the objective with the readers first. Measure it on every run, from the data, not from the job's status. A breach is the alert, even when every task succeeded. And then someone has to know who is told, who fixes it, and by when, which is section ten. Next, recovery, and the harder problem of deleting data.

Course eight showed that keeping history makes recovery possible. This section shows the other side: when data must be deleted, every copy that makes recovery possible is a copy that still holds it. The tool creates a small table of orders with a customer column and its change feed on, three orders, two of them from customer c1. It derives a total from them, one hundred, before anything is deleted. Then c1 asks to be deleted, and the table runs a delete. The terminal looks for c1 in four places. After the delete, the table holds none of c1's rows. But version one still holds both, the change feed still holds both, and the derived total still says one hundred. A delete is a new version; the old versions keep the data. Then vacuum, with zero hours of retention for the demonstration. Now version one and the change feed are unreadable: their files are gone. But the derived total still says one hundred, because vacuum only ever cleans the table it runs on. Only recomputing it makes it thirty-five. The table on the right sums up where c1 still is at each step. The list draws the tension. Retention should be long enough to recover from a bad run, and short enough that deleted data is really gone. Every derived copy needs its own recompute. And recovery has a limit too: a backfill can only replay what the source still keeps, so if a failure is noticed five days in and the source keeps seven, there are two days left to act. Next, secrets and identities.

Production is run by identities, not by people, and each identity should be able to do exactly what its job needs and nothing more. The table at the top shows three, and it is illustrative. Ana is a person: she develops in dev and reads production gold, but cannot write production tables. CI deployer is a service principal that deploys the bundle to staging and production, and cannot read customer data. Retail job is the service principal the daily job runs as: it reads bronze and writes silver and gold, and cannot deploy anything or grant access. Underneath on the left is how code should get a secret, as documented: read it at run time from a secret scope, here a partner's API password, rather than writing it in the code, where it would end up in git, in logs, and in every copy of the repository. The list on the right adds the rest. Each identity gets only what its job needs, which is least privilege. A secret is read at run time, so rotating it changes one place and nothing is redeployed. The documentation describes secret values being redacted from notebook output, but that wording is unverified here, so check it before relying on it. And remember course ten: the model found that retail job still lacks two of the grants this table gives it. Writing the table is the decision; granting it is the work. Next, who owns the pipeline, and who pays for it.

The last section of this course is about people again: who answers when something goes wrong, and who pays. The query on the left is documented, not run. It reads the billing usage system table, groups usage by a custom tag called team and by the job that used it, over the last thirty days. The result beside it is illustrative and in units, never prices. The retail data team's daily job, its pipeline, and a row with no tag at all. That last row is the warning. A cost with no tag is a cost nobody answers for, which is why the list says to tag every job and pipeline with its team, something the bundle can do for every target. The table underneath names who answers for what, again illustrative. When a run fails, the on-call engineer of the retail data team, alerted by the job's alert task from course ten. When an objective breaks, the owner of the data product, with the measurement from section seven. When a reader disputes a number in gold, the owner of gold, with the reconciliation and the lineage. And when the bill grows, the team in the tag, with the billing table. The point is to name owners before the first incident, not during it. That completes the project: built, tested, packaged, deployed, observed and owned. The final course steps back and defends the whole design.

The final course steps back from building and asks a different question: can the design be defended? Defending a design means being able to say, for each thing it promises, which component keeps that promise, and what evidence shows it does. The chain across the top is the whole project in one line. Sources: order files, order changes and the stores reference. Bronze keeps what arrived, once. Silver is typed, checked and keeps the latest row. Gold is a contract per city. And readers reach it through grants. The table underneath is the defence, one guarantee per row. The source is understood: the source contracts of course six, which are this course's assumptions, and say so. Each file is read once: the bronze checkpoint, run in course six, three, six, six, eight. No write is ever half done: Delta's transactions, run in course five. Every event is accounted for: the quality rules and the quarantine, eleven equals six plus one plus one plus three, run in course seven. Changes are applied in order: the sequence-guarded merge of course eight. Gold keeps its shape: its constraints and comments. Only the right readers see it: the grants of course four, documented and modelled, not run. And it runs every day and is watched: the job, the objectives and the owners of courses ten and twelve. The list states the discipline. Name each guarantee and the one component that gives it. Point at evidence, and say whether it was run, documented, or a model. A guarantee with no component behind it is a hope. Next, what happens when the requirements change.

A design is tested by change. This section brings two changed requirements to the project and runs both through its own modules, unchanged except for one new file. The terminal starts from the base: files a to d, gold totals one hundred and seventy. The first change is a historical correction. A new file, orders e, says order four's amount was really eighteen, not fifteen. Nothing in the code changes: silver already keeps the row from the newest file, so the correction simply wins. Silver still has six orders, York becomes eighteen, and gold totals one hundred and seventy-three. The second change is a new source. A partner sends orders keyed by a store code, L D S, Y R K, rather than our store ID. That needs the one new module, in the editor, partner dot py. It reads the partner's files as a stream with its own checkpoint, joins each code to our store ID through a small reference file, and appends the result to bronze. An unknown code becomes a null store ID, and the existing rule, unknown store, quarantines it, with no new rule needed. Silver now has eight orders, gold has Leeds four orders, one hundred and five, York two, thirty, Hull one, eighty, and the total is two hundred and fifteen. The table below the run shows the quarantine: orders seven, eight and nine, as before, and partner order three with its unknown code. And the reconciliation still closes: fifteen rows in bronze equal eight in silver, three older versions, and four quarantined. Next, choosing between the platform's ways of running a flow.

This course built the flow one way, as a job running our own modules, and showed two others along the way. The table compares the three, from the documentation and from what earlier courses ran. With a job over our code, we write the steps and their order, keep our own checkpoints, write our own quality rules and quarantine, apply changes with our own merge, and get retries and repair from Jobs. And we can test all of it locally, as the seven tests did. With a declarative pipeline, we write datasets and expectations; the pipeline keeps the streaming state, applies changes with AUTO CDC, and retries the update. The Spark inside it can be tested locally, the pipeline itself cannot. With managed ingestion, we configure a connection and its options, and the connector handles reading and retries; quality is ours afterwards. The last row is the useful one: what each leaves to you. A job leaves everything. A pipeline leaves the decisions but takes the plumbing. Managed ingestion leaves the source contract and the quality. The left list is how to choose. A supported source: try managed ingestion for bronze. A standard bronze, silver, gold flow: a pipeline. Unusual logic, or a need to test locally first: a job with code. And mixing is normal: a job can run a pipeline as one of its tasks. The right list is what no choice removes: the key, the sequence and the grain; a reconciliation readers can check; retention long enough to recover; and an owner for every table. Next, a critique of how the design fails.

A design is only as good as its behaviour on a bad day, so this section critiques it failure by failure. It starts with one more run, a changed requirement about latency: readers want silver fresher than once a day. The tool keeps silver up to date with micro-batches instead of a full rebuild: each batch's valid rows, reduced to the latest per order, merged into a fresh copy, and a row is replaced only by a newer file. The terminal applies three batches, then replays the middle one, as a retry would. Six orders, six, eight, and still eight after the replay. And the last line compares the result with the full rebuild: equal. So the latency change is safe, by the same merge pattern course eight used. The table on the right is the critique. A missing file is caught by the row-count condition of course ten. A duplicate or a replay is absorbed by a merge on the key, shown in course eight, course ten and here. Out-of-order changes are handled by the sequence guard. Lost access is found early by checking run as against the grants. Lost history is recoverable only from raw records kept in bronze. And schema drift is the weak point, which the list names. In course six, a fixed schema read twelve comma fifty as one thousand two hundred and fifty, with no error. None of this project's rules would catch a plausible wrong amount. That is a real gap, and the honest next step is a range check on amounts, or keeping unparseable values in a rescued column. Next, writing the decisions down.

The last frame is a decision record: the document that lets someone else, or you in a year, understand why the design is the way it is. The table at the top lists six decisions, each with the alternative that was turned down and the reason. Three layers, bronze, silver and gold, instead of one cleaned table, because raw data is the recovery copy. The latest row by newest landing file, instead of by event time, because these files carry no event time. Quarantine instead of drop, because every event must be accounted for. A sequence-guarded merge instead of arrival order, because records arrive late and get replayed. Liquid clustering by store instead of date partitions, because the store filter opened one file instead of seven hundred and twenty. And a job over our own modules instead of a pipeline, because it could be tested locally first. The left list states the cost assumptions, and states them as hypothetical: three seconds a file, two machines, one unit a machine-hour, twenty-four runs a day, and no price quoted anywhere. The right list is the part most records leave out: the risks still open. Silent drift, where a plausible wrong amount passes every rule. The two grants retail job still lacks. Every platform claim in this course, which must be checked against the live documentation before it is relied on. And sources that keep their data for only seven to thirty days, so a slow incident can lose data for good. This course has built one project and defended it. To go further, continue with unfamiliar sources and operating scenarios, and build practical competence through implementation experience and feedback.
